concepts.title: Post-War Return and the Mother's Belongings
concepts.definition: After the War, in Holland, the daughter of a deported Jewish mother returns to search for her mother's belongings, entrusted before the family's removal to a Mrs Dorling at number 46, Marconi Street. The address is her only thread to the objects that carry her mother's presence.
concepts.key_idea: One address, one thread to the past -- the daughter chases objects that hold a mother's touch.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp102.txt opening (after the war holland, mother's belongings, mrs dorling, number 46 marconi street)
question_patterns: why does the narrator visit number 46 marconi street

how does the war shadow the opening of the story

solution_steps.explain: Sensing danger, the mother had passed plates, cutlery and household things to Mrs Dorling, an acquaintance of wartime days.
Alone after the war, the narrator seeks these objects as the last tangible link to her mother.
The memorised address -- 46, Marconi Street -- is the entire map of her quest.

concepts.title: Two Rebukes at the Door of Mrs Dorling
concepts.definition: At the address Mrs Dorling's first reaction is denial -- staring without recognition -- and the second visit brings her daughter, who coldly explains that her mother keeps all the belongings, showing the narrator in briefly: the mother's things littered about as used, alien furniture in a stranger's parlour.
concepts.key_idea: Twice rebuffed at the door -- greed answering grief with blank stares and cold hospitality.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp102.txt middle sections (first visit denial, green cardigan knitted by mother, daughter of mrs dorling, belongings used in her house)
question_patterns: how did mrs dorling behave on the narrator's first visit
in class 11 the address: what did the narrator see inside mrs dorling's house
why did the narrator decide to forget the address

how does the author show mrs dorling's greed
what details tell us the belongings were used without care

solution_steps.explain: Mrs Dorling stares without a flicker of recognition and shuts the door -- the first rebuff.
On the second visit her daughter admits the hoard: mother's plates on the table, the burned kettle in daily use, treated as loot.
Seeing the objects stripped of their history, the narrator feels their value die in that room.

concepts.title: The Resolution to Forget the Address
concepts.definition: In her rented room the narrator resolves to forget the address -- there would be no claim on spoons and forks. The objects, cut off from her mother's living context, had turned into strangers' property; memory, not things, is the true inheritance the story finally affirms.
concepts.key_idea: Possessions recovered would be hollow -- the daughter chooses memory over furniture, and forgets the address.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp102.txt closing (resolution to forget the address, objects as strangers property, memory as true inheritance)
question_patterns: why does the narrator decide to forget the address at the end
in class 11 the address: what does the decision to forget signify
is forgetting an act of loss or of healing discuss
compare the value of the belongings before and after the war
what does the story say about material things and memory
explain the significance of the title the address

solution_steps.explain: Plates and cutlery recovered from greedy hands would carry only loss and insult, not her mother.
The mother lives in memory and in the daughter herself -- not in silverware hoarded by others.
Forgetting the address frees the narrator from a claim that could return nothing but pain.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Describe how the handling of the mother's belongings in Mrs Dorling's house differs from their life in the narrator's home.

solution_template.explain: At home each object carried use and love -- the story of the burnt kettle, plates saved for occasions, the maker's stitches in a cardigan.
In Marconi Street the same things lie about in a bleak room, used carelessly by strangers.
Objects draw meaning from their people; uprooted, they become junk -- the story's quietest lesson.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A classmate says the narrator should have fought for her mother's things. Present the case for her decision to forget the address.

solution_template.explain: Legally and morally, the belongings were hers -- a claim existed.
Recovering them returns objects already emptied of meaning, plus a quarrel with no redress.
Her mother's true presence was never in the cutlery; keeping memory and dropping the claim is the wiser inheritance.
